# Optimal ECLS Support in Mixed Cardiogenic and Septic Shock

## Abstract

Mixed cardiogenic and septic shock has been shown to have a higher mortality than cardiogenic shock alone and presents a unique hemodynamic phenotype.

This study aimed to evaluate whether higher circulatory support with veno-arterial extracorporeal life support (VA-ECLS) was associated with increased survival to discharge in patients with mixed shock.

We queried the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization database to identify adult (age >18 years) patients in mixed (cardiogenic and septic) shock requiring VA-ECLS between 2017 and 2022. Patients were categorized into lower (<2.2 L/min/m2 flow) or higher (≥2.2 L/min/m2 flow) circulatory support on VA-ECLS at 24 hours post-ECLS initiation.

A total of 452 patients supported with VA-ECLS with mixed shock were identified. Overall mortality was 63% (n = 285). Older age (adjusted OR [aOR]: 1.02; 95% CI: 1.01-1.04; P < 0.001), pre-extracorporeal membrane oxygenation cardiac arrest (aOR: 1.71; 95% CI: 1.11-2.65; P = 0.016), and baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index (aOR: 1.13; 95% CI: 1.01-1.28; P = 0.043) were associated with increased mortality. Patients receiving higher VA-ECLS support at 24 hours were numerically more likely to survive to discharge (42.6% vs 33.8%, P = 0.063). When evaluated as a continuous variable, higher VA-ECLS flow at 24 hours was associated with an aOR of 1.31 (95% CI: 0.87-1.97; P = 0.19) for survival to discharge.

Patients with mixed shock requiring VA-ECLS have a high mortality. Patients with mixed shock receiving higher support at 24 hours had a trend toward increased survival to discharge compared to those with lower support. These results are hypothesis-generating, and further studies are needed.

Key words: ECLS flow, ELSO registry, mixed shock, outcomes, VA-ECLS

## Abstract

Utilization of veno-arterial extracorporeal life support (VA-ECLS) in the treatment of refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) has increased substantially.1,2 The versatility of the VA-ECLS platform and its ability to provide comprehensive circulatory and pulmonary support has in part driven this growth.3 Optimization of VA-ECLS care in CS patients has been investigated frequently, but there remains scarce literature on the role of VA-ECLS in the management of mixed cardiogenic and septic shock.3, 4, 5, 6, 7 Patients in CS may develop concomitant septic shock, and conversely severe myocardial dysfunction in the setting of septic shock may also lead to CS.8, 9, 10 Recent studies have shown that mixed cardiogenic and septic shock is a growing problem in contemporary cardiovascular intensive care units and now accounts for 15% to 20% of patients presenting in shock. This cohort has also been shown to have higher mortality than patients with CS alone and often presents challenging therapeutic dilemmas.11,12

Effective oxygen delivery to the end organs is diminished in septic shock due to profound vasodilation and inefficient oxygen extraction. Increased cardiac output allows for improved oxygen delivery, but this compensation is generally blunted when CS is also present.13 It is reasonable to hypothesize that patients with mixed cardiogenic and septic shock who require circulatory support with VA-ECLS may benefit from higher flows. However, evidence supporting this principle is sparse and mostly limited to small series or pediatric patients with septic shock without cardiac dysfunction.14 We queried the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) database to investigate if higher circulatory support (≥2.2 L/m2) on VA-ECLS was associated with increased survival to discharge in patients with mixed shock.

## Methods

### Study population

A retrospective review was performed of adult patients (age >18 years) in the ELSO database who received VA-ECLS for cardiac support in mixed cardiogenic and septic shock between 2017 and 2022. Patients in mixed shock at the time of VA-ECLS support were identified using International Classification of Diseases-9 and 10 codes for cardiogenic and septic shock. The ELSO registry is a large international database of patients who have received ECLS, with member centers from more than 50 countries around the world.

Patients were stratified into those receiving either lower or higher circulatory support on VA-ECLS at 24 hours post-ECLS initiation. Lower support was defined as <2.2 L/min indexed to the patient's body surface area (m2). Similarly, higher support was defined as ≥2.2 L/min/m2. This cutoff was chosen as CS has previously been defined as a cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m2,15 although adequate VA-ECLS flow in mixed-shock patients largely remains unknown and is the focus of investigation for this analysis. The fundamental question we hope to answer is if indeed higher VA-ECLS flow is superior to lower flow in this cohort. Patients were excluded if they had multiple ECLS runs during index hospitalization or were discharged to a different facility while still on ECLS. Patients with postcardiotomy shock were not included in the initial database search. Patients receiving other concomitant forms of temporary mechanical circulatory support, including left ventricular unloading devices such as percutaneous ventricular assist device or intra-aortic balloon pump, were excluded because the precise magnitude of additional circulatory support provided by these devices is unknown in the ELSO registry. Additionally, mortality post-heart transplantation or durable ventricular assist device may be unrelated to VA-ECLS support prior to these interventions, and hence these patients were also excluded (Supplemental Figure 1). Center volume thresholds were established by averaging annual VA-ECLS runs per center during our study period and categorizing centers into thirds (low [≤10], average [11-25], and high [>25]). The patient's pre-ECLS Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions stage was determined based on the number of vasoactive medications and circulatory support devices patients were on prior to VA-ECLS.16

### Outcomes

The primary outcome of interest was survival to discharge during index hospitalization.

### Statistical analysis

Baseline characteristics of the patients were summarized using means and SDs for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables. The t-test was used for comparing continuous variables between the 2 groups, while chi-square test was applied to compare categorical variables. Fisher exact test was used to analyze the race variable given its small cell counts. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of outcomes, including clinically relevant variables as well as variables with two-group comparison P values of <0.10 to adjust for potential confounders. These variables included body surface area, age, pre-ECLS arrest, Charlson score, indexed pump flow, center volume, and hours on ECLS. All statistical tests were two-sided using a significance level of 0.05 with 95% CIs. Analyses were conducted using R software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

This study was deemed exempt from full review by the Institutional Review Board at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

## Results

A total of 452 patients with mixed cardiogenic and septic shock requiring VA-ECLS were identified during the study period (Figure 1). Of those, 182 (40.4%) patients were female, the median age was 51.8 (Q1-Q3: 37.9-63.9) years, and the median body mass index was 28.9 (Q1-Q3: 24.5-34.6). In the overall cohort, 159 patients (35.4%) had experienced cardiac arrest prior to VA-ECLS initiation, 203 patients (44.9%) were Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions stage D at the time of cannulation, 305 (67.5%) were cared for at a center with an annual ECLS case volume of >25, and 38 (8.4%) patients were positive for COVID-19 (Table 1 and 2).

Overall mortality among the study cohort was 63% (n = 285). A total of 152 (33.6%) patients had respiratory infection as the etiology of their septic shock, while in 234 (51.8%) patients the source remained unknown. Patients who survived to discharge were younger (47.9 vs 55.8 years, P < 0.001) and had lower body mass index (28.1 vs 29.4, P = 0.36), Charlson Comorbidity Index (1.4 vs 2.0, P = 0.001), and rates of pre-ECLS cardiac arrest (28.7% vs 39.4%, P = 0.023). Survivors were also more likely to be male (55.7% vs 44.3%, P = 0.189) and treated at high (>25 ECLS runs/year) volume centers compared to low (≤10 ECLS runs/year) volume centers (36.4% vs 31.3%, P = 0.282), although these 2 associations did not reach statistical significance (Table 2).

The most frequent complications encountered were renal failure requiring renal replacement therapy (44.2%), cardiac arrhythmias (18.8%), and cannulation site bleeding (10.8%). Rates of complications were consistently lower in the cohort that survived to discharge (Table 3). Median VA-ECLS run times were similar between survivors and nonsurvivors (142 vs 153 hours, P = 0.79).

## Discussion

In this retrospective study of patients with mixed cardiogenic and septic shock requiring VA-ECLS, we show for the first time that higher ECLS flow (≥2.2 L/min/m2) at 24 hours trended toward improved survival to discharge, although it did not reach statistical significance. Advanced age, pre-ECLS cardiac arrest, and higher baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index were all associated with lower survival to discharge. Finally, overall mortality among patients with mixed shock on VA-ECLS was worse than that historically reported for isolated CS patients requiring VA-ECLS.1

Prior studies in adult patients with septic shock supported with VA-ECLS have shown that mortality in this cohort is indeed higher than in CS alone.13,17 Septic shock may often co-exist with CS,8, 9, 10 and this mixed shock presents a unique hemodynamic phenotype that may require mechanical circulatory support to ensure adequate tissue perfusion. Like septic shock patients on VA-ECLS, our study demonstrates that patients in mixed shock are also less likely to survive to discharge (37%) as compared to previously reported outcomes in patients with CS alone (46%).1 This emphasizes the degree of clinical complexity of this unique cohort, further underscoring the importance of identifying risk factors for mortality and optimal strategies for VA-ECLS support.

One modifiable treatment strategy on VA-ECLS is the amount of circulatory support delivered. In vasodilatory shock, oxygen extraction at the tissue level is diminished, and hence an increase in cardiac output can help improve effective end-organ oxygen delivery. Our findings would suggest delivering higher circulatory support (≥2.2 L/min/m2) on VA-ECLS for patients in mixed shock may be superior to lower support at 24 hours. This is consistent with prior studies in pediatric patients with septic shock requiring VA ECLS support, in which higher flows were associated with almost twice the survival rate of standard flow ECLS.18 Importantly, targeting higher VA-ECLS flow in this cohort has clinical ramifications since it may influence cannula sizing and placement in order to increase circulatory support. Moreover, the higher flows may increase left ventricular afterload and potentially cause left ventricular distension, pulmonary edema, and aortic valve closure.

Factors associated with increased mortality in our cohort were advanced age, pre-ECLS arrest, and baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index. These risk factors all contribute to greater severity of acute illness, and indeed advanced age and pre-ECLS arrest have previously been shown to be associated with higher mortality in patients with CS.19,20 The Charlson Comorbidity Index has also been shown to predict long-term mortality in a multitude of clinical scenarios.21 While not statistically significant, it is also noteworthy that survivors were more likely to be at higher (>25 ECMO runs/year) volume centers compared to low (<10 ECMO runs/year) volume centers, highlighting the importance of clinical experience in the management of mixed shock patients. These trends highlight the clinical complexity of these patients and the need for further studies to formulate evidence-based clinical care.

### Study limitations

In addition to this being a retrospective analysis, our results should be interpreted with several limitations in mind. Firstly, the ELSO database does not capture VA-ECLS flow beyond the first 24 hours, and hence it cannot be assessed if patients received higher vs lower flow beyond that time point. We recognize that flow at a single time point may not be representative of flow throughout the ECLS run. Second, complete sets of invasive cardiac hemodynamics are unavailable in the ELSO registry to definitively establish right and left ventricular pressures and function while on ECLS support. This would especially be important to assess intrinsic myocardial output as it pertains to the total tissue perfusion. Third, the ELSO database does not consistently capture patients' post-VA-ECLS hemoglobin, which is yet another modifiable component of the total oxygen-carrying capacity. Fourth, the ELSO database does not capture the timing and sequence of diagnosis of each type of shock, which would be important in understanding the clinical course of these patients. Additionally, the rationale for lower VA-ECLS support, namely clinician decision or clinical circumstances, cannot be identified through the database. Finally, we cannot show causality in this observational analysis, and hence our findings should be considered hypothesis-generating specifically for patients in mixed septic and CS and not broadly in all CS patients with concomitant vasoplegia. We cannot exclude residual confounding.

## Conclusions

In our study, patients with mixed shock requiring VA-ECLS had a high mortality. Patients with mixed shock who received higher support at 24 hours had a trend toward increased survival to discharge compared to patients who received lower support. These results are hypothesis-generating and highlight the need for further studies in this field.

COMPETENCY IN PATIENT CARE: Patients with mixed (cardiogenic and septic) shock who require VA-ECLS support have higher rates of mortality than those VA-ECLS patients with CS alone.

TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: In this cohort, higher flow through the ECLS circuit may possibly give patients a higher likelihood of surviving to discharge.
